title: Capstone: Physical AI
blurb: Tests why a capstone measures the integration gap, how noisy perception limits a safety monitor, checking sensor noise before trusting downstream results, scoping a capstone, and turning a measured residual risk into a deployment decision.

ideas.title: A safety layer is bounded by its inputs

§66.2.1 Why This Matters More Than a Clean Result Would

questions.prompt: What question does this capstone answer that no single chapter could?
options: Which single component is the most accurate on its own?
Which cloud service should host the robot's model?
How fast can a policy be trained in simulation?
Does the whole system still work with every part imperfect at once?
questions.explanation: Each earlier chapter isolated one piece with clean inputs. The capstone combines them and measures what changes at the boundaries.

questions.prompt: In Procedure 66.2, what is the integration gap?
options: The number of components left untested
Combined collision rate minus the isolated one
The difference between training and test loss
The time it takes to connect two components together
questions.explanation: The same safety monitor is evaluated with perfect and with noisy perception. The difference shows what the combination costs.

questions.prompt: The safety monitor's logic didn't change between chapters 65 and 66. Why did collisions rise from 0 to 2?
options: The policy got worse between the two chapters.
The test states were made harder in chapter 66.
It acted on noisy positions, not ground truth.
The monitor's clearance threshold was raised.
questions.explanation: A safety layer's guarantee is bounded by the quality of what feeds it. Correct logic on uncertain input still leaves residual risk.

refLinks.label: §66.2.2 A Safety Layer’s Guarantee Is Bounded by What Feeds It

questions.prompt: Why check the sensor's measured noise before evaluating the pipeline?
options: The safety monitor can't run without a noise estimate.
A noise mismatch silently breaks tuned components.
Noise checks speed up the policy's inference.
Sensors always report less noise than they really have.
questions.explanation: Procedure 66.1's common mistake is trusting documented noise. Here the measured σ was about 0.15, matching the assumption, so downstream results could be trusted.

questions.prompt: The sensor's measured std was [0.1509, 0.1451] against an assumed 0.15. What does the chapter conclude?
options: The y-axis sensor is broken, since it differs from x.
The sensor is biased and must be recalibrated first.
The noise model holds well enough to trust.
The noise is too low, so the test is unrealistic.
questions.explanation: Both are close to 0.15, and the mean is close to the true position. The check passes before anything else is evaluated.

questions.prompt: What scope does the chapter recommend for a capstone?
options: A small task, with every stage present
Only the stage the builder finds most interesting
Large in task complexity, done in one impressive stage
Each chapter's code chained together with no new measurement
questions.explanation: Too ambitious and each piece is shallow. Too safe and nothing is combined. Chaining without measuring teaches nothing new.

refLinks.label: §66.2.3 What a Real Capstone Project Looks Like

questions.prompt: The combined pipeline had 2 collisions in 40 trials. What residual collision rate is that, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: 2 / 40 = 0.05, or 5%, the number Procedure 66.3's deployment plan is built around.

questions.prompt: What deployment decision does a 5% residual collision rate lead to?
options: Ship autonomous, but only to a 5% canary group.
Ship fully autonomous, since the monitor cut collisions sharply.
Cancel the project, since any collisions are unacceptable.
Ship human-supervised until the risk is reduced.
questions.explanation: Nonzero residual risk means a person stays in the loop. This is not the decision chapter 65's noiseless 0/40 would have supported.

questions.prompt: The monitor cut collisions from 11/40 to 2/40 under noisy perception. What percentage of collisions did it prevent? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: (11 − 2) / 11 = 0.818, or 81.8%. A large reduction, but short of chapter 65's 100% with perfect perception.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call the 2/40 result more useful than a clean 0/40 would have been?
options: It's the real number a decision needs.
It proves the safety monitor is badly designed.
It shows noisy perception makes policies better at the task.
It is easier to explain to stakeholders than zero.
questions.explanation: Real systems don't get perfect inputs. Measuring the residual, and deciding from it, is the skill. The task success rate stayed 0/40 in every configuration.

bookExercises.prompt: State the specific integration question this capstone asks that no single earlier chapter was built to answer.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Whether the whole pipeline still works when every piece, perception, policy, safety layer, is realistically imperfect at once, not just tested one piece at a time against clean/idealized inputs for the other pieces.

bookExercises.prompt: State the three measured collision numbers from the Worked Example (no monitor, noisy+monitor, Chapter 65's noiseless+monitor) and rank them from most to fewest collisions.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: No safety monitor (noisy perception): 11/40 collisions. With safety monitor (noisy perception): 2/40 collisions. Chapter 65's noiseless + safety monitor: 0/40 collisions. Ranked most to fewest collisions: no monitor (11) > noisy + monitor (2) > noiseless + monitor (0).

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's measured residual (2/40 collisions with noisy perception + safety monitor, versus 0/40 with perfect perception + the same monitor), explain what this comparison proves about where the safety monitor's guarantee actually comes from. Is it the monitor's own logic alone, or something more?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The comparison proves the safety monitor's real-world guarantee is NOT determined by its own logic alone. The monitor's rule/code is identical between the 0/40 (Chapter 65) and 2/40 (this chapter) results, yet the outcome differs solely because the input feeding it changed from perfect to noisy. This demonstrates that a safety layer's actual guarantee is bounded by the quality of everything feeding it. Correct monitor logic is necessary but not sufficient for a specific numeric safety guarantee; the guarantee also depends on the accuracy of what it's monitoring.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 66.1's sensor-characterisation check (measured std 0.1509/0.1451 vs. assumed 0.15), explain why this verification step had to happen BEFORE trusting the 2/40 collision result, not after.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The sensor-characterisation check had to happen first because the entire 2/40 result is only trustworthy if the noisy sensor actually behaves the way the pipeline assumes it does. If the sensor's real noise were, say, std=0.4 instead of the assumed 0.15, the safety monitor (tuned assuming 0.15 noise) might be systematically under- or over-cautious, and the 2/40 number would reflect a mismatched, unrepresentative test rather than a genuine measurement of the monitor's real-world performance. Verifying the measured noise (0.1509/0.1451) matches the assumed model (0.15) first confirms the downstream 2/40 result is actually measuring what it claims to measure.

bookExercises.prompt: A team that individually validated their perception system, policy, and safety monitor separately, each performing well in isolation, wants to skip integration testing and ship directly, reasoning "each piece works, so the combination will too." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own capstone found exactly the gap that reasoning misses: the safety monitor reached 0/40 collisions when tested against perfect perception, but only 2/40 when tested against the same policy and monitor with realistic noisy perception feeding it. Each piece worked in isolation, but the combination revealed a real residual risk neither isolated test could show. Integration testing isn't redundant with component testing; it answers a different question, and skipping it means shipping with an unmeasured, potentially much worse than assumed, real-world failure rate."

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 66.3's deployment-plan logic, explain concretely why "the safety monitor achieved 0/40 collisions in Chapter 65's testing" would be the WRONG number to cite when writing a real deployment plan for this capstone's pipeline.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Citing "0/40 collisions" from Chapter 65's testing would be the wrong number because that result was measured under perfect, noiseless perception, a condition this capstone's own combined pipeline does not actually operate under. Using it in a real deployment plan would understate the actual residual risk (2/40, or 5%) by an entire order of magnitude, giving false confidence that the system is fully safe when the honestly-measured, realistic-conditions number shows it isn't, exactly the "safety layer is not a fix" trap Chapter 65 warned about, recurring here at the level of citing the wrong measurement rather than skipping a safety layer entirely.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Book 1's Data Science Lifecycle chapter's framing of iterative validation. Explain in your own words how this capstone's finding (a safety guarantee degrading once combined with a realistic, imperfect upstream component) is an argument for validating a full pipeline repeatedly as components change, rather than validating each component once and assuming the combination is permanently safe.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Iterative validation treats "this component passed its test" as provisional, not permanent, valid only under the specific conditions it was tested against, and requiring re-validation whenever those conditions change (new data, a new upstream component, a changed noise profile). This capstone's finding is a direct instance of that principle: the safety monitor's Chapter 65 validation was correct and permanent for noiseless perception, but became stale/insufficient the moment it was combined with a different (noisy) upstream component. The guarantee didn't transfer automatically. This argues for treating "the safety monitor is validated" as a claim scoped to specific tested conditions, and re-running the full combined pipeline's validation whenever any upstream component (sensor, policy, environment) changes, rather than treating a one-time component-level pass as a permanent system-level guarantee.
